tasks.q: Match each description to a level.
pairs: A binary instruction word executed by a CPU
tasks.fb: Mnemonic instructions are readable labels for low-level operations. The examples are not a real processor specification.

tasks.q: Which statement about assembly-style instructions is correct?
a: Mnemonic names represent low-level operations
The CPU directly reads every mnemonic as English
The same assembly instruction set exists on all CPUs
They remove the need to understand instruction order
tasks.fb: Mnemonic source is more readable than binary, but still closely reflects a processor design.

tasks.q: The accumulator is 3. ADD 4 is executed. What is its new value?
tasks.fb: In this model ADD combines its operand with the value already in the accumulator.

tasks.q: After SET 5, then SET 2, what is in the accumulator?
tasks.fb: SET replaces the previous value. It does not add to it.

tasks.q: Build a program that displays 7 by adding 3 and 4, then step until it halts.
Which step sends the working value to the output?
a: EMIT
SET
ADD
HALT
tasks.fb: The teaching processor only displays a value when EMIT executes.

tasks.q: In this model, ADD 4 has operation bits 0010 and operand bits 0100. Which word encodes it?
tasks.fb: Place the operation field first, then the four-bit operand. This is not a real CPU encoding.

tasks.q: Why should you not send this invented encoding to an arbitrary real CPU?
a: Its instruction format and operation codes may be different
Real CPUs never use binary
Four bits always mean a letter
A mnemonic is identical to an electrical signal
tasks.fb: An instruction only has meaning within the instruction set and encoding designed for its processor.

tasks.q: Repair the out-of-order program so it displays 7, then step through the corrected version.
A trace reaches the wrong result without any invalid instruction. What kind of problem is likely?
a: A logic error in the sequence
Proof that the CPU cannot add
A spelling error must exist
A broken screen must be the cause
tasks.fb: A valid sequence can still implement the wrong algorithm.

tasks.q: What does the workshop mainly demonstrate?
a: High-level tasks can be represented as smaller processor operations
All real processors have exactly four instructions
Every high-level statement is one byte
Assembly programming is compulsory for J277
tasks.fb: The model is deliberately small and original. Its instruction set is enrichment, not required recall.

tasks.q: Which job most clearly benefits from precise low-level control?
a: A carefully optimised routine that must manipulate particular hardware resources
A project whose only requirement is easy editing by beginners
A document with no executable instructions
A page of revision notes
tasks.fb: Specific hardware requirements can justify extra implementation detail.

tasks.q: Why is machine code described as processor-dependent?
a: Its binary instruction patterns belong to a particular instruction set
All CPUs understand identical operations
It is always written in Python
It contains no operands
tasks.fb: Different architectures can assign different meanings to the same binary pattern.

a: Assembly-style mnemonics are more readable than binary but remain close to hardware
Assembly source is executed as English
Machine code is independent of hardware
A high-level language cannot calculate
tasks.fb: Both machine code and assembly are low-level; mnemonics help humans read the operations.

info.title: Three views of one job
info.text: A high-level statement describes the intended calculation. Assembly-style mnemonics expose small processor operations. Machine code encodes operations and their data in binary. Think: Why can a short high-level calculation require several CPU instructions?

info.title: Meet the teaching processor
info.text: This original model has one accumulator, which holds the working value. The instruction pointer identifies the next instruction. SET replaces the working value; ADD changes it; EMIT displays it; HALT stops execution. Think: In the workshop, how is the accumulator different from the output?

info.title: Build and trace
info.text: Select the operation in each slot before stepping through the program. Track the accumulator and next instruction after each step. The model is enrichment: OCR J277 does not require this instruction set or assembler knowledge. Think: Build a program that adds 3 and 4 and displays 7. Record the accumulator after each step.

info.title: Encode an instruction
info.text: Our invented instruction word contains four operation bits and four operand bits. SET uses operation bits 0001; ADD uses 0010. This encoding belongs only to the teaching model; real CPUs use their own formats. Think: Using the displayed encoding, explain the two parts of 0010 0100.

info.title: Diagnose the sequence
info.text: Correct operations in the wrong order can give the wrong output. A trace helps locate the first difference between expected and actual behaviour. Changing the instructions means the previous trace is no longer evidence for the new program. Think: A program emits 3 before adding 4. Why is its displayed result not 7?

info.title: Control has a cost
info.text: Working close to the processor exposes small operations explicitly. That control can be useful, but there is more detail to manage. For J277, focus on language characteristics and translation; the simulator makes those ideas visible. Think: Why is this four-step example not evidence that all high-level code is inefficient?
